findings.title: A real application start loads a second copy of the application through the backend.app root
findings.status: FIXED — verified inside app/; declared stateless residual in shared/
findings.description: A real create_app() loaded 36 backend.app.* modules — a second copy of the application inside the same process, including a second kernel, a second config, and a second database module with its own Base and its own Engine. NR-050 repaired the capability share (10 capability.py files), bringing it to 34 and removing the second kernel. The residual belongs to app/national/task_engine (13 modules) and app/national/workflow_runtime (14), plus services/governance, services/reference and integration/connectors/email.py.
findings.root_cause: Dockerfile:24-26 copies the application twice — `COPY backend ./backend` alongside `COPY backend/app ./app` — so from WORKDIR /app both `app.x` and `backend.app.x` resolve to the same file as two distinct module objects, each with its own module-level globals. Modules that name the backend.app root then bind to the shadow copy.
findings.evidence: `import app.kernel.integration as a; import backend.app.kernel.integration as b; a is b` → False with identical __file__. app/kernel/integration.py:15 holds `_kernel_instance` as a module-level global. Counted live: 36 shadow modules before the NR-050 repair, 34 after. The shadow Base carries 0 tables and the shadow engine is unused, so nothing has diverged yet. | NR-058 CLOSURE: the residual was 73 import statements across 25 files in five packages (national/task_engine 27, national/workflow_runtime 37, services/governance 5, services/reference 3, integration/connectors 1), plus one module path passed as a string -- engineering/performance/benchmark.py benchmarked the import time of 'backend.app.kernel', which an AST guard cannot see. After the rewrite a real create_app() loads 2 shadow modules, down from 34, and both are namespace packages on the way to backend.app._compat, imported by shared/ (which lives at the repository root, outside backend/). _compat holds constants: no engine, no session factory, no declarative base, no registry, so the duplicate cannot diverge. That exemption is itself tested.
findings.security_impact: None demonstrated. No authorization or tenancy path runs through the shadow tree today.
findings.clinical_impact: None today. The hazard is silent divergence: state written through one copy is invisible to the other, and a capability registering through the shadow kernel would succeed while reaching nobody.
findings.recommended_fix: Permanent fix is the container layout — stop copying the application twice. Correcting the task_engine and workflow_runtime import roots is a package-wide change with its own review. Neither was done under NR-050, whose brief forbade a repository-wide import migration.
findings.verification: backend/tests/test_capability_import_roots.py holds the repaired capability tree and carries the residual as DECLARED_SHADOW_ROOT_PACKAGES — a ledger that may shrink but never grow, with a per-entry test that fails if a listed package is repaired and left in the list.
findings.next_batch: unscheduled — DECISION REQUIRED on container layout
findings.minimal_safe_fix: APPLIED: `backend.app.` -> `app.` across the five packages. No behaviour change intended and none measured: 1787 OpenAPI paths before and after, the same 42 task/workflow endpoints registered. The container layout (Dockerfile:24-26 copying the application twice) is still the root cause and is unchanged; the repair removes every in-process consequence of it under app/.
findings.verification_method: backend/tests/test_capability_import_roots.py, widened: the AST ledger is empty and no longer exempts engineering, and the behavioural test now asserts a real create_app() loads no second copy of any *stateful* module, not just the kernel -- the three that matter are the kernel (redirects registration), app.database (splits the connection pool) and any declarative base (hides tables from Alembic and conftest). Negative-proven: restoring one import in task_engine/infrastructure/models.py fails both the static and the behavioural test.

findings.title: 42 registered endpoints are served by fifteen tables that no migration builds
findings.description: factory.py registers the task_engine (23 paths) and workflow_runtime (19 paths) routers. Their repositories read and write fifteen tables -- national_tasks, national_task_queues, national_task_assignments, national_task_escalations, national_task_sla_definitions, national_task_comments, national_task_audit_logs, national_workflow_definitions, national_workflow_executions, national_workflow_execution_steps, national_workflow_approvals, national_workflow_timers, national_workflow_compensations, national_workflow_templates, national_saga_logs -- and no migration in the chain creates any of them.
findings.root_cause: Same shape as NR-022: a domain was modelled and exposed before its schema was built. What is specific here is that NR-058's import defect hid it. Both packages registered their models on a second NationalBase reached through the backend.app root, so test_schema_fidelity's ORM surface -- the gate whose entire purpose is to inventory ORM tables with no migration -- never saw them and was under-counting by fifteen.
findings.evidence: grep of every file in backend/migrations/versions for each of the fifteen names: no match. create_app() OpenAPI schema: 1787 paths, of which 42 are under /national/tasks and /national/workflows. Importing one repository module loads a second app.database with its own Engine against the same URL, so these paths would also have run outside the documented pool budget (WEB_CONCURRENCY x (DB_POOL_SIZE + DB_MAX_OVERFLOW)). | NR-059 CLASSIFICATION: 51 handlers across the two route modules, 42 unique OpenAPI paths. Registration corrected: these are registered DIRECTLY at factory.py:695/698, not via national_router (which is unregistered — that is why the NR-060 consent stub is unreachable while these are live). Exactly 2 handlers touch no repository (/national/tasks/health, /national/workflows/health) and work today; the other ~40 each reach a service -> repository -> one of the 15 unbuilt tables. They are NOT placeholders: the packages contain domain entities, enums, domain events, repository interfaces, SQLAlchemy implementations, a workflow state machine and a saga engine — a complete implementation that was never given a schema. A CONSUMER EXISTS: frontend-v3 pages NationalWorkflowRuntimeApiPage.tsx and NationalTaskEngineApiPage.tsx issue ten queries against these endpoints, so on a migrated database those pages return server errors. Four of the ten are additionally malformed with a double slash where a path parameter belongs (/executions//steps, /executions//approvals, /tasks//comments, /tasks//history) — the NR-054 auto-generated-page signature. These pages are a different class from NR-057: they resolve to registered routes that cannot return data.
findings.clinical_impact: Workflow and task routing are coordination surfaces, not clinical record surfaces; no patient record is at risk. A caller relying on a task being persisted would be wrong about it.
findings.security_impact: None identified — the endpoints authenticate before reaching persistence.
findings.data_integrity_impact: No data is written, so none can be corrupted; nothing is durable.
findings.operational_impact: 42 endpoints are advertised in the OpenAPI schema that cannot complete a persisted operation on a migrated database.
findings.dependencies: NR-022 (the National Core is unbuilt as a whole); NR-058 (which hid this).
findings.recommended_fix: Classification complete; the remaining question is product intent and is not derivable from the repository: is national task/workflow orchestration a feature GULA ships, or scaffolding that was generated and never removed? Shipping -> build the 15 tables in one migration and fix the four malformed frontend URLs; ownership (NR-051) and implementation already exist, making this the cheapest of the NR-022-family decisions. Not shipping -> retire both packages and both frontend pages, shrinking the National Core problem by 15 tables. What must NOT happen is building 15 tables so 42 endpoints stop erroring without deciding whether anyone wants the feature. Separately, under NR-054's rule the two frontend pages should be hidden until that resolves — recommended, not applied, because it is an API-surface change.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: NOT ATTEMPTED. What was done is to make the state visible and keep it visible: the fifteen tables are now declared in test_schema_fidelity's unbuilt ledger with the endpoint count stated, so the next model added to these packages is a review rather than a silent addition.
findings.verification_method: backend/tests/test_schema_fidelity.py — the ledger entry fails if any of the fifteen acquires a migration and the entry is left behind, and the gate now sees the ORM surface it was always meant to.
findings.acceptance_criteria: Either the fifteen tables are migration-backed, or the 42 endpoints are not registered.
findings.regression_risk: Low for the declaration; the decision itself is Medium.
findings.evidence_strength: STRONG (migration chain searched by table name; endpoint count from a live OpenAPI schema)

findings.status: DECIDED — canonical owner established; dormant fail-open stand-in guarded, not executed
findings.title: Consent had eight implementations across six domains and no stated canonical owner
findings.description: Seven ORM classes map seven distinct *consent* tables (consents, niam_consents, niam_lifecycle_consents, trust_consent_records, dp_consent_directives, national_consents, rp_consent_records) and an eighth implementation, citizen_platform.privacy.ConsentEngine, is not an ORM model at all. No two share a table, so this was never NR-051's one-table-two-owners problem; it is eight concepts sharing a word.
findings.root_cause: Consent was modelled independently by each domain that needed it, with no constitution naming which store an authorization decision must consult.
findings.evidence: Cached 829-class ownership scan re-queried for 'consent': 7 ORM classes, 7 tables, 6 domains, zero duplicate table ownership. Migration search by table name: only 4 of 7 are built (consents 20260417_0001, niam_consents 20260814_0006, niam_lifecycle_consents 20260723_0002, trust_consent_records 20260716_0013); the other 3 are ORM-only and all three are already declared in test_schema_fidelity's unbuilt ledger. Live OpenAPI from create_app(): 16 of 1787 registered paths mention consent. Decisive evidence for ownership: exactly one implementation is wired into an authorization decision -- security/consent_dep.py::require_consent is a route dependency guarding services/mpi/api.py:316, and it queries `consents` via services/consent_service.py. It is also the only one that audits: log_access_decision writes an AuditLog row on all five decision branches (owner bypass, emergency denied, emergency allowed, no-consent deny, allow). Subject/tenancy columns measured per table: consents keys on gpid (citizen ULID) + grantee_id with no tenant column; trust_consent_records is the only one carrying lab_id.
findings.affected_components: app/models/consent.py, app/services/consent_service.py, app/security/consent_dep.py, app/identity/models/consent.py, app/identity/lifecycle/models.py, app/trust/models.py, app/citizen_platform/privacy.py, app/national/security/consent_enforcement.py
findings.affected_users: Any actor reading citizen data through a consent-gated path
findings.clinical_impact: Consent gates citizen data reads and carries doctor-only emergency break-glass. The canonical path is intact; no clinical path was found reading a non-canonical store.
findings.security_impact: Two dormant hazards, neither live. (1) ConsentEnforcementService returns granted=True for any input and its log_consent_check is `pass` -- fail-open with no audit. It is unreachable for two independent reasons: factory.py does not register national_router, and its only call site passes citizen_id= to a parameter named patient_id while omitting the required requestor_id, so it would raise TypeError. (2) ConsentEngine stores consent in a process-local dict, so a grant is lost on restart and invisible to other gunicorn workers; nothing authorizes on it, so it misinforms rather than mis-authorizes.
findings.data_integrity_impact: None found; the canonical store's invariants are the strongest of the eight.
findings.operational_impact: Eight consent surfaces mean a caller can grant consent somewhere that the enforcement path will never read.
findings.legal_impact: Consent is a legal artifact in this domain. A grant recorded in a non-enforced store is evidence of an intent the system does not honour.
findings.dependencies: NR-050 (this was its last blocked disposition), NR-051.
findings.recommended_fix: CANONICAL OWNER: app/models/consent.py::Consent over table `consents`, written through app/services/consent_service.py and enforced by app/security/consent_dep.py. Chosen on evidence -- it is the only store an authorization decision consults, the only one that audits every outcome, and the only one with break-glass semantics. Consolidating the other seven is NOT recommended as a single step: niam_consents (account-to-account grants), trust_consent_records (lab-scoped, the only tenant-scoped one) and niam_lifecycle_consents (person lifecycle) are different relations, not copies, and merging them would be an irreversible data decision.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: APPLIED, additive only: backend/tests/test_consent_canonical_ownership.py records the decision as an executable invariant. No consent code was changed. Specifically NOT done: correcting the ConsentEnforcementService call signature, because a correct call to a fail-open service is strictly worse than a broken call to one -- the guard ties the two facts together instead, so the service must fail closed before that router may be registered.
findings.verification_method: 5 tests: the consent-table ledger is exact both ways; each declared migration still builds its table; the enforced path resolves to `consents` and audits all five branches; a fail-open consent service must not be reachable; and no enforcement module consults the in-memory ConsentEngine. Negative-proven by registering national_router in factory.py -- the reachability test fails with the intended message and passes again on restore.
findings.acceptance_criteria: One consent store is named canonical and no permissive stand-in is reachable.
findings.regression_risk: None from this change; it adds tests and alters no runtime code.
findings.evidence_strength: STRONG (live OpenAPI, migration chain by table name, enforcement call graph read end to end)

findings.status: DECIDED — canonical composition named; rival registries guarded, not built
findings.title: Practitioner is modelled seventeen times; the only built natural-person registry is the Identity Platform's
findings.description: 17 ORM classes model practitioner/provider/staff/employee/healthcare-worker/person. Only 4 are built, and 3 of those 4 are homonyms: fin_providers (financial service provider), pay_providers (payment processor), niam_fed_providers (OIDC/SAML identity provider). Exactly one built table represents a natural person: niam_persons. Every clinical variant is unbuilt, including national_practitioners -- at 88 foreign-key references the single most-depended-on table in the repository.
findings.root_cause: Each domain modelled its own practitioner rather than composing the Identity Platform's, and NR-022's framing ('the most-depended-on tables do not exist') invites closing the gap by building them.
findings.evidence: Cached 829-class ownership scan filtered for person-like concepts (17 classes), cross-referenced against an AST parse of every op.create_table in the migration chain (evidence-created-tables.json, 419 tables). Column-level comparison: national_practitioners flattens into one row what the Identity Platform models relationally and has BUILT -- niam_persons (full_name, date_of_birth, gender, nationality, phone, email, national_id_hash), niam_licenses/ProfessionalLicense (license_number, issuing_authority, expiry_date, board_certification), niam_employments/Employment (person_id -> organization_id, position, dates), niam_assignments (posting) and niam_role_assignments (permissions). The Identity Platform is 84 of 87 tables built. One genuine gap: specialty/sub_specialty has no equivalent in niam_licenses, which carries license_type and board_name only.
findings.affected_users: Every clinical path that names a practitioner
findings.clinical_impact: Practitioner identity underpins attribution of clinical acts and licence validity at the time of care.
findings.security_impact: Building a rival registry would copy name, date of birth, phone, email and national ID hash outside the proofing, assurance and verification governance that surrounds niam_persons, and would contradict CLAUDE.md's rule that the Identity Platform is the single trusted identity provider.
findings.data_integrity_impact: Two person registries cannot be reconciled without a matching strategy; none exists.
findings.operational_impact: 88 foreign keys name a table that does not exist.
findings.legal_impact: Duplicated personal data enlarges the custodianship surface.
findings.recommended_fix: CANONICAL: a practitioner is not an entity. It is a Person (niam_persons) who holds a ProfessionalLicense (niam_licenses) and an Employment (niam_employments) / Assignment (niam_assignments), with permissions through niam_role_assignments. Do NOT build national_practitioners. Re-pointing its 88 references is an architectural change that depends on the NR-022 subject/identifier decision and is not attempted here. The one real additive gap -- clinical specialty -- belongs on niam_licenses, not in a new table.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: APPLIED, additive only: backend/tests/test_practitioner_canonical_identity.py asserts the canonical composition is still built and that no rival person registry has acquired a migration. Retiring the rivals stays allowed; building one fails the gate. No code changed.
findings.verification_method: 4 tests: the created-table evidence is present and plausible (>=400 tables); the canonical composition is migration-backed; no rival person registry is built; the rival ledger still names real ORM tables. Negative-proven by marking national_practitioners as built in the evidence file -- the guard fails with its intended message and passes again on restore.
findings.acceptance_criteria: One registry of natural persons, and it is the Identity Platform's.
findings.regression_risk: None; tests only.
findings.evidence_strength: STRONG (column-level comparison against a migration-derived built-table set)

findings.status: MEASURED — corrected and double-ratcheted (package + module). Stage 1 rollout applied
findings.title: CLAUDE.md requires every mutation to be audited; 328 mutating endpoints are in packages with no audit call at all, and 1065 are in modules with none
findings.description: The audit architecture itself is sound and needs no redesign: services/audit_service.py chains each entry as SHA-256(previous_chain_hash + record), anchors it off-database under an HMAC (AUDIT_ANCHOR_KEY) and can re-verify the chain (verify_audit_chain). That is tamper-evident. Coverage is the gap. Of 1222 mutating endpoints (POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE) across 42 packages, 271 (22%) are in 25 packages containing no audit call anywhere. Corrected in Unit 4: the original 271/25 figure was produced by a detector matching its tokens as plain substrings, which counted `query_audit_log(`, `access_audit_log(`, `get_audit_log(` (app/control_plane -- three read helpers) and `_write_audit` (app/governance) as canonical audit calls. Word-boundary matching restores both packages: 27 packages, 328 endpoints. Measured per module instead of per package, 130 of the 160 modules containing a mutating endpoint contain no audit call, covering 1065 of 1222 endpoints -- the upper bound, now ratcheted alongside the lower one.
findings.root_cause: The rule is stated in CLAUDE.md but enforced nowhere mechanically: auditing is a call each author must remember to make, at the layer furthest from the mutation.
findings.evidence: AST scan of app/ counting POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE route decorators per package, against a broad token search for audit participation. 271 unaudited mutating endpoints across 25 packages is the LOWER bound -- 'the package audits somewhere' does not prove a given endpoint audits. A module-level pass gives the upper bound: 435 of 527 route-module endpoints (83%) are in modules that never name an audit call. Both are proxies and are reported as such. Highest-count unaudited packages: payments 34, capabilities 29, document_intelligence 25, ai_fabric 23, blood_bank 21, research_platform 16, devices 15, critical_care 14. 21 audit-like tables exist in the ORM, 12 built, but only audit_logs carries the chain.
findings.affected_components: app/ (25 packages); canonical chain in app/services/audit_service.py
findings.affected_users: Anyone relying on the audit trail to reconstruct who changed what
findings.clinical_impact: blood_bank (21 unaudited mutating endpoints) and critical_care (14) are traceability domains: blood product lifecycle and infusion changes are exactly what an audit trail exists to reconstruct.
findings.security_impact: An audit trail with a 22% floor of unaudited mutations cannot answer 'who changed this', and the hash chain's tamper-evidence applies only to what was written to it.
findings.data_integrity_impact: Mutations outside the chain are unreconstructable after the fact.
findings.operational_impact: Incident reconstruction and compliance evidence are incomplete by an unknown margin.
findings.scalability_impact: Session-level enforcement would add one insert per audited mutation; the chain is already serialized on last-hash read.
findings.legal_impact: ISO 27001 A.8.15 is cited in the audit service docstring; partial coverage weakens that claim.
findings.dependencies: NR-045 (canonical audit write repair, VERIFIED), NR-060 (consent audits all five decision branches).
findings.intersections: NR-045, NR-060, NR-021. NR-065 (the package blind spot this now measures around: app/national counts as auditing because interop.py does, while task_engine and workflow_runtime contain no audit call). NR-066 (what app/governance writes instead).
findings.contradictions: CLAUDE.md security invariant #2 states all mutations MUST write to the audit log; measurement shows at least 22% do not.
findings.recommended_fix: ENFORCE AT THE SESSION, NOT THE ROUTE. The mutation classes that must produce audit evidence are: clinical result/order state changes; authorization decisions including break-glass; identity lifecycle and role assignment; consent grant/revoke; blood product and controlled-substance lifecycle; financial and billing mutations; tenant/scope changes; and bulk export or disclosure of patient data. Enforcing per route has failed for 271 endpoints because it depends on an author remembering. A SQLAlchemy before_flush hook over a declared set of audit-worthy tables cannot be forgotten, sees the actual INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE, and can reuse infrastructure that already exists: database.py maintains per-request contextvars (request_id, endpoint, user_id, lab_id) for error correlation, which is exactly the actor context an audit row needs. NOT implemented here -- it changes write behaviour on every session and needs its own review.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: APPLIED, additive only: backend/tests/test_audit_chain_invariant.py ratchets the measured gap. Each declared package may shed unaudited mutations; none may gain them, no new unaudited package may appear, and a resolved entry must be removed rather than left as a stale allowance. The chain's own integrity (chain hash, previous-hash link, HMAC anchor, verifier) is asserted too, because the invariant is only worth enforcing while the chain is real. No runtime code changed.
findings.verification_method: 7 tests. Package ratchet (declared per-package counts, no new package, no stale entry), chain-integrity assertion, and a module-level aggregate ratchet. Negative-proven by removing app/governance from the ledger -- the guard fails naming it, proving the detector correction is load-bearing -- and by adding an unaudited mutating module, which fails the module ratchet with '131 modules ... up from 130'. Both restored byte-identical.
findings.acceptance_criteria: Every mutation class listed above produces a hash-chained audit entry, enforced where it cannot be forgotten.
findings.regression_risk: None from this change; tests only. The recommended session hook carries real risk and is deliberately not applied.
findings.evidence_strength: STRONG for the lower bound (AST over the whole route surface); the upper bound is explicitly a proxy

findings.status: LATENT — precondition guarded; blocks any schema build under these create paths
findings.title: 103 create paths splat an unvalidated request body into an ORM constructor; 75 set no tenant or actor
findings.description: Found while trying to resolve NR-022's nine REVIEW sites. They could not be decided from their call sites, and the reason mattered more than the question: the call sites are generic passthroughs. A route takes a bare `data: dict` with no request model and hands it to `Model(**data)`. Measured across app/: 103 such constructions. 28 set tenant and/or actor server-side; 75 set neither, so the request body would decide every column including lab_id, verified_by and is_deleted.
findings.root_cause: Create paths were written as untyped dict passthroughs, so neither validation nor server-side tenancy has anywhere to live.
findings.evidence: AST scan for `Model(**param)` where param is a function argument, cross-referenced against the migration-derived built-table set. 103 sites; unguarded concentrated in care_continuum_service (40), clinical_service (18), ehr_service (17). The defensible pattern is `ClinicalTask(lab_id=lab_id, created_by=user_id, assigned_by=user_id, **data)` -- tenant and actor come from the authenticated user, a colliding body key raises TypeError rather than overriding, and those paths audit. CRITICAL SAFETY FACT: zero of the 75 unguarded sites targets a built table, so every such write currently fails with UndefinedTable before a row exists. The pattern is latent, not live. Detector note: server-setting occurs in two forms -- an explicit keyword and a pre-splat `data['key'] = value` mutation. The first version of this scan counted only the former and reported create_compliance_check as unguarded when it does set the actor by mutation; corrected before shipping, which moved the split from 27/76 to 28/75.
findings.affected_components: app/services/care_continuum_service.py, app/services/clinical_service.py, app/services/ehr_service.py, app/routes/care_continuum.py (41 `data: dict` routes)
findings.affected_users: None today — the target tables do not exist
findings.clinical_impact: Latent. If these tables were built, a caller could assert clinical attestations (verified_by, assessed_by) it did not make.
findings.security_impact: Latent tenant assignment: the 75 unguarded models are TenantAuditEntity subclasses, so lab_id would come from the request body rather than the authenticated user, contradicting CLAUDE.md security invariant #1. Blocked today only by the absent schema.
findings.data_integrity_impact: Latent: id, is_deleted and audit columns would be caller-settable.
findings.operational_impact: Blocks NR-022 and NR-059 schema work until the create paths are fixed.
findings.legal_impact: Latent: forged attestation of clinical review.
findings.dependencies: Blocks NR-059 activation and any National Core table build.
findings.intersections: NR-022, NR-059, NR-021 (the same tenant-isolation class, which was live there).
findings.contradictions: CLAUDE.md invariant #1 requires tenant scoping from current_user; these paths take it from the body.
findings.recommended_fix: Per create path: a Pydantic request model instead of `data: dict`, and tenant/actor set server-side from the authenticated user rather than accepted from the caller -- the pattern nhdw and hospital already use. Fix the path, then build the table; either order is fine, only the omission is unsafe.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: APPLIED, additive only: backend/tests/test_passthrough_write_precondition.py makes this a precondition rather than a prohibition. A table may not be built while its create path is an unguarded passthrough, no new unguarded module may appear, no declared module may gain sites, and the guarded pattern must not disappear. No runtime code changed.
findings.verification_method: 4 tests: the scan still finds >=90 passthrough constructions; no unguarded passthrough reaches a built table; the unguarded ledger does not grow; the guarded pattern still exists. Negative-proven by marking cc_risk_stratification built in the evidence file -- the precondition fails naming (table, module, function) and passes again on byte-identical restore.
findings.acceptance_criteria: Every create path validates its input and sets tenancy server-side before its table is built.
findings.regression_risk: None from this change; tests only.
findings.evidence_strength: STRONG (AST over the whole service surface, cross-referenced with migration-derived built tables)

findings.status: FIXED — VERIFIED. citizen_id resolves to the canonical person and carries a real foreign key; patient_id is refused pending NR-022
findings.title: The citizen-relationship create endpoint queries national_citizens and national_patients, neither of which exists, and reports the failure as a generic 500
findings.description: POST /admin/citizen-relationships is registered at factory.py:599 and reachable by any actor holding platform:manage_users with ministry authorization. Its workflow validates the subject by querying `Citizen` (national_citizens) and, when a patient is named, `Patient` (national_patients). Neither table is created by any migration, so on a migrated database the query raises UndefinedTable before a row is ever written. The route catches `Exception` and returns 500 'Citizen relationship workflow failed', so the operator is told the workflow failed but not that the schema is absent.
findings.root_cause: niam_citizen_relationships was built ahead of the National Core subject tables it references. The migration guards the foreign keys on `_has_table(target)` -- correctly, or a fresh database could not migrate -- but the service still validates against the ORM class unconditionally.
findings.evidence: app/routes/citizen_relationship_admin.py:69 (POST) -> app/identity/services/citizen_relationship_service.py:144 `self.db.query(Citizen).filter(Citizen.id == citizen_id)` and :152 for Patient. app/national/domain/citizen.py / patient.py map to national_citizens / national_patients; both are absent from the migration-derived evidence-created-tables.json. Registration proved at factory.py:561/599. The FK-creation guard is at migrations/versions/20260811_0002_citizen_relationship_foundation.py:68-83.
findings.affected_users: Ministry administrators using the citizen-relationship workflow; indirectly every citizen whose delegate access depends on it
findings.clinical_impact: Guardian, caregiver and delegate access to a citizen's record cannot be granted through the canonical workflow.
findings.security_impact: No bypass introduced -- the path fails closed. The risk is the opposite: an access-granting workflow that cannot run invites an out-of-band substitute.
findings.data_integrity_impact: None today: nothing is written. The two declared columns carry no database-level referential integrity because the migration could not create the constraints.
findings.operational_impact: The failure surfaces as an undifferentiated 500, so the cause is not visible to the operator who hits it.
findings.legal_impact: Delegated-access consent cannot be recorded through the intended audited path.
findings.dependencies: Blocked by the absence of national_citizens / national_patients (NR-022).
findings.intersections: NR-022 (this is the entire live surface of the 263 subject references), NR-059 (same class: a registered route over an unbuilt table), NR-054.
findings.contradictions: The workflow is otherwise exemplary -- explicit keywords, idempotency key, optimistic version, hash-chained audit -- which is why the missing schema is easy to miss. The workflow's own test suite was green throughout: it hands the service a fake session whose query() returns a SimpleNamespace, which cannot notice that the table behind a model does not exist. That is why the new guard is static.
findings.recommended_fix: Decide the canonical subject for citizen_id and patient_id per NR-022 (CITIZEN and PATIENT classes respectively), build or re-point to that owner, then create the two foreign keys in the same migration. Separately, let the route distinguish 'schema absent' from 'workflow failed' so the 500 names its cause.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: APPLIED. (1) `create_pending` resolves the subject against `app.identity.models.person.Person` (`niam_persons`) instead of `national_citizens`, with linkability read from the person's own `is_deceased`/`is_active`. (2) `patient_id` is refused with CitizenRelationshipUnsupported (422) rather than queried against the unbuilt `national_patients`; the column is left in place so NR-022's clinical-subject decision stays open. (3) The ORM foreign key is re-pointed to `niam_persons.id`. (4) Migration `20260914_0001` creates that foreign key fail-closed: it counts rows whose citizen_id does not resolve and refuses with the count rather than casting, defaulting or deleting anything. The constraint it replaces could never be created -- the foundation migration guards it on _has_table.
findings.verification_method: 3 regression tests plus a static guard. `test_reachable_unbuilt_reads.py::test_the_citizen_relationship_workflow_reads_only_built_tables` pins both modules at zero unbuilt reads; negative-proven by restoring the pre-fix service, which fails naming [('Citizen','national_citizens',144), ('Patient','national_patients',152)]. Two behavioural tests cover the patient_id refusal and person linkability. NR-022's distribution ratchet independently caught the change (CITIZEN 75 -> 74) and its live-reference ledger shrank from two entries to one. PostgreSQL behaviour of the migration is verified by the CI migration gate (apply head, downgrade -1, upgrade head).
findings.acceptance_criteria: POST /admin/citizen-relationships either succeeds against a real subject table or is withdrawn; no registered write path queries an unbuilt table.
findings.regression_risk: None from this change; tests and documentation only.
findings.evidence_strength: STRONG (call graph read end to end; registration and build status both from committed evidence)

findings.title: 14 of the 15 national orchestration tables have no tenant column and neither package reaches the audit chain
findings.description: NR-059 left activation blocked on product intent. Unit 3 ran the checks the approved decision actually gates on and found two more blockers that do not depend on that question. All 15 task and workflow tables extend `BaseEntity` -- the one national base carrying neither TenantMixin nor AuditMixin, while TenantEntity, AuditEntity and TenantAuditEntity all exist alongside it. Only national_workflow_executions has a tenant column. The task listing path filters on status, priority, category, assignee, queue_id and a title LIKE, and on nothing else, because there is nothing else to filter on. Neither package contains a call reaching the hash-chained audit log, and there is no idempotency key or row lock anywhere in a package containing a saga engine and a workflow state machine.
findings.root_cause: The two packages were implemented against the bare BaseEntity rather than TenantAuditEntity, and were never given a schema, so neither the tenancy gap nor the audit gap was ever exercised.
findings.evidence: AST over app/national/task_engine and app/national/workflow_runtime: 15 tables, 1 with a tenant column (national_workflow_executions). national_tasks has 22 columns and no tenant scoping of any kind. Zero word-boundary matches for log_action / audit_service / AuditLog( / log_access_decision in either package. national_task_audit_logs has 6 columns (task_id, action, actor_id, previous_status, new_status, details) -- no chain hash, no previous-hash link, no off-database anchor. WorkflowExecutionRepository.save loads by id, mutates and commits without reading `version`.

findings.status: CORRECTED and LATENT — the audit row cannot be written and nothing calls the code; guarded as a precondition
findings.title: The governance repository base writes an audit row into an unbuilt table from every create, update and delete
findings.description: CORRECTION to this finding's first record, which said governance 'writes rows; they are the wrong rows' and that 'rows exist, which is worse than none in one respect: it reads as coverage'. They do not exist and cannot. `gov_health_number_audit` is built by no migration, so the `HealthNumberAudit(...)` that `GovernanceRepository._write_audit` constructs from `add`, `update` and `delete` would raise UndefinedTable on flush -- taking the caller's own governance row down with it, because six of the tables its subclasses serve ARE built (gov_break_glass_accesses, gov_guardians, gov_identity_records, gov_merge_proposals, gov_qr_codes, gov_recovery_requests). The reason it has never happened is that nothing calls those repositories: their two persistence services are imported by no module outside app/governance/services, and the registered governance_router imports nine other service modules instead. The original observations still stand where they apply -- it is not the hash-chained AuditLog, the actor is the literal string "system", and the row is a health-number audit whatever entity was mutated -- but they describe code that cannot run rather than rows that exist. Severity lowered from P1 to P2 on that evidence.
findings.root_cause: A domain-specific audit model was wired into the generic repository base, and the authenticated actor was never threaded through to it.

findings.title: 483 query sites read, and 147 constructions write, tables no migration builds; 267 reads are reachable from a registered route
findings.description: NR-064 turned out to be one instance of a platform-wide class. Measured across app/ with model names resolved through each file's own imports: 483 `query(Model)` sites name a table no migration creates, concentrated in app/national (203), app/insurance (150) and app/services (103). Of those, 267 are reachable from a registered router -- in the route module itself or one import hop away, which is exactly NR-064's shape, since that route was clean and its service was not. The worst reachable modules are routes/clinical.py (57), routes/clinical_quality.py (55) and national/scheduling_platform (41). Each is an endpoint that raises UndefinedTable the first time it is called and reports whatever its error handling reports. The write side was measured alongside it: 147 ORM constructions target an unbuilt table -- app/services 77, app/national 43, app/insurance 20 -- and writes fail differently from reads. A read raises UndefinedTable and returns nothing; a write raises it on flush and takes the caller's own rows with it. NR-066 is the instance that showed the difference.
findings.root_cause: Whole subsystems were implemented against ORM models that were never given a schema, and nothing asserted that a reachable read resolves to a built table. Fake-session unit tests cannot detect it, because a fake answers query() regardless of whether the table exists.
findings.evidence: AST scan of app/ resolving each queried name through the file's ImportFrom statements, cross-referenced with the migration-derived evidence-created-tables.json; registered routers parsed from factory.py. Import resolution is load-bearing: 32 ORM class names in this repository map to more than one table (Citizen -> mpi/models.py and national/domain/citizen.py; Patient -> patients and national_patients), and a bare-name scan reported 838 sites against the true 483 -- a 42% false-positive rate -- while silently missing NR-064's own Citizen line because the built homonym won the lookup.

findings.security_impact: Fails closed -- the query errors rather than returning data. The risk is operational opacity and the pressure to 'fix' it by creating tables without an activation review.

findings.operational_impact: Endpoints that cannot work are indistinguishable from endpoints that are merely failing, because the error surfaces as a generic 500.

findings.intersections: NR-064 (the first instance, now repaired), NR-059, NR-065, NR-054, NR-063.

findings.recommended_fix: Per module, decide: build the table under the §6 activation review (canonical owner, tenancy, actor, audit, state machine, idempotency, consumers), or stop reading it and withdraw the endpoint. Do not create tables to make the detector green.
